title: HTTP and HTTPS: methods, headers and status codes

videos.script: Five lessons of machinery, and none of it said anything. Wires, addresses, layers, envelopes — all of it built to carry something, and we have not yet looked at what. {{so-far}} This is what. {{reveal}} That is a complete request. Not a summary of one, not a diagram: those are the actual characters your browser sent, and you can read them. A word, a path, a version, and a few lines naming what you are and what you will accept. {{read-it}} The answer comes back the same way. A number, a few lines, a blank line, and then the page. {{response}} Two things follow from that, and both matter more than they look. The first is that you can type this by hand. People do, to test things, and you will before this lesson ends. {{by-hand}} The second is that a protocol you can read is a protocol you can debug. Every network problem in the rest of this course is something you will be able to look at directly rather than guess about. {{debug}} What the lesson covers is the vocabulary: which word to use for which action, what the number means, what the lines in between are for, and what changes when an S is added to the name. {{title}}

The padlock in the address bar. Everybody knows it means secure. Almost nobody can say what it promises, and the gap between those two is where people get hurt. {{padlock}} Start with what a certificate is. A document saying: this public key belongs to this name. Signed by somebody. {{document}} Which is worth exactly as much as the signature. So whose is it? {{whose}} Here is the chain. Your site's certificate is signed by an intermediate. The intermediate is signed by a root. And the root is signed by nobody at all — it is simply in a list your browser shipped with. {{chain}} That list is the whole foundation. A few hundred organisations your browser has decided to believe, chosen by the people who made your browser, and you have almost certainly never looked at it. {{list}} Now the part that matters. What does a valid certificate actually prove? {{question}} It proves that whoever is answering controls this name. That is all. {{all}} It does not say the site is honest. It does not say the company is real. It does not say your data is handled well on the other side. A site set up this morning to take your card details gets a padlock in about a minute, free, and it will be a real one. {{not-honest}} That is not a flaw in the system. It is the system working: the padlock answers the question am I talking to who I asked for, which is a different question from should I trust them. {{different-question}} What it does rule out is somebody in the middle. The café's network cannot read this, the provider cannot change it, and nobody between you and the name on the certificate can pretend to be it. {{middle}} That is a great deal, and it is not the same as safe. {{close}}
